lines.text: from time to time the fountain of his heart is unsealed as he
observes the beauties of nature, then he once more comes
clearly to realize that his life stands under higher laws and
springs from a deeper foundation on which it remains
dependent. Then there steals into his heart some surmise of
the true dimensions of his being. And when he seeks refuge
from the noise and bustle of the world in the silent spaces of
nature, then the sense of eternity may once more emerge into
his consciousness:
"When over the silent plain the moon's sickle swings, the
heart that shudders in anguish is released from its pain.
Eternity is silence. Change is feverish clamour. Silently
sweeps God's will over the distant spaces of earth."1
Man can do many things. He can create great beauty in
painting and sculpture, he can raise mighty buildings to
embody his soaring fancies. And yet when he opens his being
to the majesty of the mountains or the mysterious power of
the sea, he may be swept by the sense of the pettiness of the
artistic works which he creates in comparison with the over-
awing splendour and sublimity of the works of nature. And
considering the beauty of the flowers of the field he may
grow deeply aware that even Solomon in all his glory was not
arrayed like one of these (Matt. 6: 29).
Man can do many things. He can raise monuments of his
skill which last for decades and even for centuries. And the
greatest of his monuments retain an abiding worth for the
successive generations. But they do not escape the law of
transience and decay. Whole civilizations come to maturity
and die, and nothing abides eternally. The work of man's
hand passes away; but nature goes on its unvarying course
throughout all ages, renewing its life with every spring and
scattering lavishly its riches without ever becoming poorer. The
sun of Homer smiles on us too, and the angels praise the Lord:
"And all your noble works are grand
As if on that first day, creation's dawn, they stand."
